## Pulse sequences: Spin echo (Hahn)
<!--
![Pulse sequences: Spin echo (Hahn). The hare-and-tortoise analogy shows how a 180° refocusing pulse reverses phase coherence: fast ("hare") and slow ("tortoise") spins that have dephased by TE/2 are flipped and return into phase at time TE (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 5.10).](images/ch09/pulse-sequences-spin-echo-hahn.png){#fig-ch09-pulse-sequences-spin-echo-hahn}
-->

In our last two chapters, we explored T1 and T2 relaxation separately. But in real MR experiments, you'll typically see both effects mixed together!

The magic happens in what we call the "pulse sequence" - the carefully timed dance of RF pulses and gradients that determines how these relaxation effects combine.

In this chapter, we'll dive into one of MRI's most important tricks: the spin echo. You'll see how we use multiple RF pulses to isolate the T2 signal in a simple experiment that's as elegant as the FID we started with.

## The RF pulse sequence up to now (FID)

![The RF pulse sequence up to now (FID).](images/ch09/the-rf-pulse-sequence-up-to-now-fid.png){#fig-ch09-the-rf-pulse-sequence-up-to-now-fid}

After the RF excitation pulse, we can measure a macroscopic signal (the FID).  That's a start.  But notice that the signal starts very quickly and decayse very quickly.  That makes it hard to instrument in real applications, particularly ones where we have to make a lot of measurements, say scanning a volume.

## Spin Echo (Hahn)

![Spin Echo (Hahn).](images/ch09/spin-echo-hahn.png){#fig-ch09-spin-echo-hahn}

The Hahn echo was not only a method to remove static dephasing; it introduced the idea that magnetic resonance signals could be engineered in time, allowing detection to be separated from excitation. This temporal separation was essential for overcoming hardware limitations and made practical NMR—and later MRI—possible.

For the original papers and biographical material, see the resource [Erwin L. Hahn and the Spin Echo](resources/erwin-hahn.qmd).

## Single spin echo: Signal

<!--
![Single spin echo: Signal.](images/ch09/single-spin-echo-signal.png){#fig-ch09-single-spin-echo-signal}
-->

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![The spins dephase; at a certain point they are flipped 180° (B1 pulse) so the leading phases become lagging; they re-phase, producing the echo at time TE.](images/ch09/single-spin-echo-formation.mp4){#vid-ch09-single-spin-echo-formation width="70%" loop="true" autoplay="true" muted="true"}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
![The spins dephase, are flipped 180° (B1 pulse), and re-phase to produce the echo at time TE (video; see the HTML version for the animation).](images/ch09/single-spin-echo-formation.png){#vid-ch09-single-spin-echo-formation width="70%"}
:::

Viewed in the rotating frame, the spins dephase.  If we apply a 180 deg pulse, the leading phase becomes the lagging phase.  Since it is going faster, it catches up.  The spins reaphase and form an echo.

## Multiple echoes
<!--
![Multiple echoes.](images/ch09/multiple-echoes.png){#fig-ch09-multiple-echoes}
-->

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![Repeating the 180° pulse produces multiple echoes; the peak of each echo declines over time because of spin-spin (T2) relaxation, and the decay of the echo amplitudes measures the pure T2 decay.](images/ch09/multiple-spin-echoes-decay.mp4){#vid-ch09-multiple-spin-echoes-decay width="70%" loop="true" autoplay="true" muted="true"}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
![Repeating the 180° pulse produces multiple echoes whose peak amplitudes decay with T2 (video; see the HTML version for the animation).](images/ch09/multiple-spin-echoes-decay.png){#vid-ch09-multiple-spin-echoes-decay width="70%"}
:::

It is possible to repeat the 180 deg flip several times, forming multiple echoes.  

* The peak of each echo declines over time because of the usual spin-spin (T2) decay
* The decay of the echo amplitudes measure the pure T2 signal
* Multi-echo measurements are widely used in resting state measurements

:::{.callout-note title="Multi-echo measurements"}
I will explain ways in which multi-echo measurements may be useful in a later section.  I will also point to software packages that help investigators analyze the multi-echo data.  
:::
